questions.question_text: A 29-year-old newly married female with significant depressive symptoms, including insomnia and weight loss, was noncompliant with medications in the past due to sexual dysfunction.
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine is a typical antidepressant with noradrenergic and serotonergic activity. Its mechanism of action includes blockade of the α2-adrenergic auto- and heteroreceptors, as well as blockade of the 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors and histaminergic (H1) receptors. This unique combination results in increasing serotonin, and, in higher doses, norepinephrine; however, mirtazapine doesn't create sexual dysfunction and, especially at lower doses, causes sedation and increased appetite.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with severe major depression on high dose of antidepressant develops increase blood pressure.
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine is an antidepressant that inhibits the reuptake of both serotonin, and, in higher doses, norepinephrine. Because of this, it may cause increased blood pressure, particularly in doses above 300 mg daily.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old divorced female being treated for major depression doesn't refill her prescription in 2 days later she has chest, muscle aches, and nausea.
questions.explanation: Although most antidepressants can cause withdrawal syndrome (characterized as flu-like symptoms) if abruptly discontinued, those with shorter half-lives, especially paroxetine, are more likely to do so.

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old woman with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) has history of poor compliance with medications, occasionally missing doses.
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine has significantly longer half-life than the other listed antidepressants. This translates into fewer "withdrawal" symptoms if suddenly stopped and may be an advantage in cases of occasional poor compliance.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old woman recently diagnosed with first episode of schizophrenia agrees to take antipsychotic medication to help decrease her hallucinations, but she is notably opposed to taking any medication that causes her to gain excessive weight. Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate to prescribe?
questions.explanation: Most of the second-generation antipsychotics cause weight gain, including clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone. However, ziprasidone, lurasidone, and aripiprazole are weight neutral.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old married female without past psychiatric history is referred by her internist. She has been feeling "down" for several weeks, with little ability to enjoy herself. Since that time, her sleep has been disrupted, her appetite reduced, and she's felt "tired." She has also been making mistakes at work and is worried about being fired. She admits to having thoughts of killing herself, but she denies any plan or intent to do so. She denies hallucinations or delusions. Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient is suffering from major depressive disorder (MDD), single episode. While there are many efficacious antidepressants to choose from, serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as citalopram are considered first-line treatment.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents to her primary care doctor complaining of sudden onset of intense fear and feeling that she was going to die, which occurred while she was stuck in traffic earlier in the week. At that time she became short of breath, diaphoretic, and tremulous and she could feel her heart pounding. Her initial impulse was to drive to an emergency department, but her distress subsided on its own in about 20 minutes. Which of the following should be the next most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Conduct thorough medical screening for heart and lung disease.
Prescribe selective-serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and ask to see the patient back in 1 week.
Prescribe short-acting benzodiazepines as needed in case of another episode.
Reassure the patient that her symptoms most likely benign and not cause for concern.

correct_answer.text: Conduct thorough medical screening for heart and lung disease.

correct_answers.text: Conduct thorough medical screening for heart and lung disease.

questions.explanation: Panic attacks are characterized by sudden onset of intense fear, terror, or anxiety, and accompanied by a variety of physical symptoms. Although virtually any organ system can seem to be the source of distress in panic disorder, common symptoms include shortness of breath, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremulousness, flushing, chest pain, and dizziness. Regardless of the clinical setting or psychiatric history, patients presenting with symptoms suggestive of panic disorder must be thoroughly worked up to rule out physiologic pathology as the source of the symptoms.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 45-year-old man with history of schizophrenia. He is currently compliant with his antipsychotic medications but remains psychotic, with auditory hallucinations and paranoia. On mental status examination (MSE), he speaks coherently and articulately, but keeps no sense because any of the words he uses are of his own invention. Which of the following terms best describes this MSE sign?
questions.explanation: Neologistic speech, positive symptoms of schizophrenia, consists of words created by the patient having no established meaning.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old woman presents to psychiatrist with 6-year history of emptiness and depression for "most of the time," with low self-esteem, chronic insomnia, and difficulty making decisions. She denies any problems with her appetite or energy, and, while she does not feel like her condition will improve, she denies any suicidal ideation. She drinks one to two drinks once or twice per month, but denies illicit drugs. She is subsequently begun on fluoxetine, which is gradually increased to 60 mg. She denies side effects, although she has not experienced significant lessening of her depressive symptoms. How long should her current dosage be continue before switching to another medication?
questions.explanation: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is chronic, low-level depression that lasts for at least 2 years in adults. While treatment with an adequate trial (on typical dose) of an antidepressant should last at least 6 weeks before deciding that it is failure.

questions.question_text: A 56-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol for many years. She denies any current psychotic symptoms and has been compliant with her medications. She presents for routine follow-up appointment. Which of the following tests should be administered?
questions.explanation: The AIMS is the standard clinical examination and rating scale that should be administered to patients receiving antipsychotics (neuroleptics) such as haloperidol. It is useful for detecting the development of tardive dyskinesia as well as tracking changes over time.

questions.question_text: An brings his wife to the doctor because she has become more psychotic over the past several weeks. She is diagnosed with schizophrenia and has recently stopped her medications. She has threats toward her husband because she believes that he is an impostor who looks exactly like her husband. Which of the following terms best describes this symptom?
questions.explanation: Patients with Capgras syndrome suffer the delusion that someone familiar is an identical-appearing replacement.

questions.question_text: A 69-year-old woman without prior psychiatric history is seen by her primary care physician due to "crying spells." She states that she has felt sad since the sudden death of her husband 5 weeks ago. Since that time, she has had difficulty sleeping and fatigue. She has also lost several pounds due to not enjoying her food. She is able to cheer up when spending time with her children, but feels especially lonely at night. She is somewhat anxious because she occasionally hears her deceased husband's voice, especially early in the morning or late in the evening. While she feels her future is "bleak," she denies any suicidal ideation or plan. Which of the following diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bereavement is the psychological reaction to loss, often the death of a significant other. While symptoms may overlap with MDD (depression, appetite/sleep/energy changes), the intense symptoms of depression in bereavement are often short-lived and self-limiting, and there is little overall functional impairment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes this symptom?
questions.explanation: Copropraxia is a complex motor tic occasionally seen in Tourette disorder, characterized by making obscene gestures.

questions.question_text: While obtaining the history, the patient is also noted to repeat phrases you use immediately after you say them. Which of the following terms best describes this symptom?
questions.explanation: Echolalia refers to repeating another's words or phrases; it is sometimes seen in catatonia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnosis is the most likely?
questions.explanation: Kleptomania is an impulse control disorder where individuals steal objects not out of need or monetary value.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms relates to the fact that these impulses are distressing to her?
questions.explanation: Ego-dystonic refers to whether thoughts or behaviors are distressing to the patient.

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old man comes to you complaining of headaches, memory loss, disorientation, and occasional paralysis that affects his legs and lasts several hours. During the mental status examination, you notice that the patient is giving vague answers to any questions (e.g., there are six toes on the foot and 2 + 2 = 5). Which of the following terms best describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome was thought to be type of dissociative disorder, characterized by giving approximate answers.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist discovers that she is frustrated and easily angered with one of her patients for no obvious reason. While talking to colleague, she admits that the patient reminds her of her abusive father. Which of the following best describes the clinician's reaction?
questions.explanation: Countertransference refers to feelings the patient elicits in the therapist, versus transference, which refers to feelings the therapist elicits in the patient.

questions.explanation: Kayser–Fleischer rings are one such physical sign in Wilson disease: golden brown or gray-green rings of pigment at the corneal limbus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes the abnormal movements seen in this patient?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus is an uncontrolled swinging of an extremity associated with Wilson disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following ter s best describes the belief that the patient’s thoughts toward the neighbor were responsible for the lost Pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Magical thinking and ideas of reference are two types of delusions found in psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes the patient's fear that her thoughts could be overheard?
questions.explanation: Thought broadcasting is the delusion that one's thoughts can be heard by others, often seen in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate diagnosis for this patient?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

questions.explanation: This patient is currently experiencing manic episode. Bipolar I disorder includes manic episodes with or without depressive episodes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate to prescribe?
questions.explanation: Mood stabilizer (such as valproic acid or lithium) is first-line treatment for bipolar I disorder manic or mixed episodes.

questions.question_text: A 36-year-old woman was begun on alprazolam (Xanax) 3 years ago for panic disorder. After watching news report on television, she became frightened about addiction. She abruptly stopped the medication 2 days ago and has since been experiencing acute, intense anxiety, tremors, sweating, and palpitations. Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate to prescribe?
questions.explanation: The most efficacious treatment for benzodiazepine withdrawal is to use benzodiazepine with long half-life (e.g., diazepam) and to slowly taper it over time.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnoses would be the most appropriate in this ptient?
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder) is often dramatic onset of neurologic symptoms that likely result from unconscious conflicts.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes this patient’s minimization of the severity of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: La belle indifférence is the classic lack of concern shown toward deficit or loss of function sometimes seen in conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder).

A 67-year-old woman with pulmonary carcinoma and secondary brain metastases recently drafted a will in the presence of her family attorney. She has a history of major depressive disorder (MDD) that is now in remission. She decides that her children who are well established in their careers do not need any inheritance and that her estate would best serve charity. To secure the validity of the will, the patient asks her psychiatrist to submit a letter to her attorney regarding her competency.
Which of the following would be the most important factor in determining this woman's testamentary capacity?

options.text: The presence of a conservator of person
The presence of a judge to witness the signing of the will

questions.explanation: The run on letter test, which relies on concentration, cooperation, and the ability to hear, is the test of choice. It consists of telling patient a letter and then in monotone voice listing a string of letters. The patient responds by raising finger to indicate when he or she hears the key letter. The other tests rely not only on attention but also on calculation abilities and therefore education level.

questions.question_text: You are consulted to see a 77-year-old Hispanic male with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, admitted to the hospital for chest pain. His workup has revealed pulmonary embolism, and the medical team wishes to place chest tube in the patient, but the patient refuses. The primary team has asked you to determine his capacity to refuse the procedure. Which of the following features is the most important in determining decision-making capacity in this patient?
questions.explanation: Capacity, which is situation- and time-specific, is a frequent psychiatric consult question. Elements of capacity include the ability to communicate one's wishes, to understand one's illness, to understand the risks and benefits of treatment and nontreatment, and to reason about one's options.

questions.question_text: A deputy sheriff serves you subpoena for the records of one of your patients who is the defendant in a civil liability lawsuit. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Release the patient's records to the plaintiff because the subpoena overrides patient consent.
Hand over only the information that is relevant to the case.
Contact the patient and ask if she or he would like the information released.
Release the patient's records directly to the court.
Refuse to speak to the sheriff in order to maintain confidentiality.

correct_answer.text: Contact the patient and ask if she or he would like the information released.

correct_answers.text: Contact the patient and ask if she or he would like the information released.

questions.explanation: Physician–patient privilege should be breached only in specific instances such as patient initiates litigation, consent to release information is obtained, there is a duty to protect, emergency situation, or in cases in which the court orders release. Contacting patient and asking is appropriate here.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old graduate student you have been seeing in long-term psychotherapy has stopped paying his bills, despite being reimbursed by his insurance company. Which of the following is the next most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Contact the patient’s insurance company and request that they issue you another payment.
Directly address this issue with the patient at the next scheduled appointment.
Inquire with family members whether the patient has financial problems.
Notify collection agency to obtain reimbursement.
Send the patient letter of termination.

correct_answer.text: Directly address this issue with the patient at the next scheduled appointment.

correct_answers.text: Directly address this issue with the patient at the next scheduled appointment.

questions.explanation: When a patient stops paying bills, the physician should directly address the issue with the patient who may have underlying issues for which the patient has entered into psychotherapy or that relate to psychiatric symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnoses is the most likely in this case?
questions.explanation: Malingering is the intentional production of symptoms for secondary gain (e.g., to avoid work, social or legal obligations).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best describes the above patient’s production of symptoms and motivation?

options.text: Conscious production of symptoms to assume the sick role.
Conscious production of symptoms to obtain secondary gain.
Unconscious production of symptoms due to unconscious conflicts.
Unconscious production of symptoms to obtain secondary gain.
Unconscious production of symptoms to assume the sick role.

correct_answer.text: Conscious production of symptoms to obtain secondary gain.

correct_answers.text: Conscious production of symptoms to obtain secondary gain.

questions.explanation: In malingering, the symptoms are consciously produced to obtain secondary gain.

questions.question_text: You are asked to evaluate a 68-year-old man on the inpatient medicine service for increasing confusion. The patient was admitted 2 days earlier for pneumonia. After performing mental status evaluation, you suspect delirium. Further history from the patient’s wife indicates that the patient dropped out of school in the seventh grade. Which of the following tests would best assess his ability to maintain and focus attention?
questions.explanation: In this instance, the random letter test, which relies on concentration, cooperation, and the ability to hear, is the test of choice. It consists of telling a patient a letter and then in a monotone voice listing a random string of letters. The patient responds by raising a finger to indicate when he or she hears the key letter. The other tests rely not only on attention but also on calculation abilities, and therefore educational level.

questions.question_text: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of sore throat and fever. Her parents took her to the pediatrician's office about 1 week ago and he recommended fluids and bed rest. Within the last 2 days, the patient developed dysphagia, severe drooling. His parents indicate the patient has been anxious and impulsive over the last month. There has also been marked decline in school performance, and she has not been interested in playing with her friends. Physical examination is remarkable for significant erythema over the posterior pharynx with gray exudate. There are abrasions in the region of the patient's lips. Complete blood count shows white blood cell (WBC) count of 14,000/µL with left shift. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step?

options.text: Arrange for family meeting to determine if sepsis is osition.
Contact the state's Child Protective Services while keeping the patient safe.
Detain the parents while you notify the police.
Notify the probate court to have the patient legally remove from the alleged perpetrator.
Refer the patient to the family psychiatrist.

correct_answer.text: Contact the state's Child Protective Services while keeping the patient safe.

correct_answers.text: Contact the state's Child Protective Services while keeping the patient safe.

questions.explanation: When sexual abuse of a child is suspected, the first step is to ensure the safety of the child immediately and notify the state's Child Protective Services. Reporting is mandatory in cases of physical and sexual child abuse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Administer thiamine orally (PO) before IV fluids and glucose.
Administer thiamine intravenously (IV) before IV fluids and glucose.
Administer thiamine IV after IV fluids and glucose.
Administer naloxone IV before IV fluids and glucose.
Administer naloxone IV after IV fluids and glucose.

correct_answer.text: Administer thiamine intravenously (IV) before IV fluids and glucose.

correct_answers.text: Administer thiamine intravenously (IV) before IV fluids and glucose.

questions.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy, condition seen in chronic alcohol use disorders, results from acute thiamine deficiency and presents with the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. It is important to administer thiamine parenterally prior to glucose administration because glucose and fluids first may worsen symptoms resulting in permanent damage.

questions.question_text: The above patient is stabilized and admitted to the ICU. After 3 days, he begins to become confused again, with visual hallucinations, tremors, diaphoresis, and elevated blood pressure and pulse. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing symptoms consistent with severe alcohol withdrawal, namely delirium tremens (DTs), characterized by delirium, confusion, combativeness, and elevated vital signs. The treatment of choice is intramuscular or intravenous benzodiazepines.

questions.question_text: A young white male, age unknown, is brought into the emergency room unresponsive to questioning. His vitals demonstrate normal temperature, low pulse and blood pressure, and decreased respirations. He appears lethargic, with pupils that are constricted and initially responsive. Administration of which of the following would be most likely to improve his condition?
questions.explanation: Opioid intoxication is characterized by the triad of somnolence, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils. Opioid intoxication can be rapidly reversed with intravenous administration of an opioid antagonist, such as naloxone.

questions.question_text: A 77-year-old woman without prior psychiatric history is brought into her family physician's office with her husband. He is concerned that she is "depressed" and needs treatment. He describes her with waxing emotionality over the past year or two, with gradual decline in her ability to care for herself. They have been unable to take part in their usual social activities, and the patient "just wanders around the house during the day." He has also noticed that she is forgetful, often misplacing items, and mixing up names of acquaintances. When asked, the patient denies any difficulties, stating she feels "fine," and that her husband worries too much. She adamantly refutes problems with her memory, instead blaming him for moving things around in their house. She has no significant medical problems. Upon MSE, she is less attentive and cooperative with questions, although defensive at times. Her affect is neutral but full. There is no suicidal or homicidal ideation, and she denies any psychotic symptoms. Her Mini-Mental State Examination is 20/30. Her physical is essentially unremarkable.
questions.explanation: This woman is showing signs of a major neurocognitive disorder (dementia), likely due to Alzheimer disease, the most common cause of neurocognitive disorders (dementia). The primary treatment modality is to begin an anticholinesterase inhibitor, such as galantamine. Memantine, an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist, is a medication that may be added to the regimen additionally, but it is not as effective in mild dementias. Antidepressants (e.g., citalopram) and antipsychotic medications (e.g., ziprasidone) may be used for associated depression or agitation/psychosis, respectively, but they are not primary treatments. Ginkgo biloba has not been shown to be effective for the memory deficits in neurocognitive disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following characteristics increase this particular patient's risk of committing suicide?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for complete suicide include (1) age > 45, (2) male gender, (3) never married > widowed/separated/divorced > married, (4) white race > black race, and (5) religious > not religious.

questions.question_text: The patient waits until her family and primary care team leave the room. She then asks you to help her commit suicide, as her prognosis is very poor. What is the most appropriate next course of action?

options.text: Discuss her reasons for suicide in more detail.
Explain how she can obtain lethal doses of medication.
Refer her to physician who performs euthanasia.

correct_answer.text: Discuss her reasons for suicide in more detail.

correct_answers.text: Discuss her reasons for suicide in more detail.

questions.explanation: Physician-assisted suicide involves the doctor's facilitating person's death by providing the information or equivalent necessary to end his or her life. The AMA's Code of Medical Ethics strongly condemns such action as fundamentally incompatible with the physician's role as healer.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman who scores 26/30 on the Folstein MMSE gives many answers of, "I don’t know, I’m too tired to answer." You want to assess for the possibility of depression.

options.text: Weschler Test (This is likely a typo and should be Wechsler)

questions.explanation: The Beck Depression Inventory (A) is a 21-item test with three responses per item that is an easily used screening tool to evaluate for depression. Because it would be unusual for an individual so young to have a major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) and because many of the answers reflect a lack of interest, the Beck Depression Inventory, in conjunction with the Folstein MMSE, may help distinguish depression from dementia.  The WCST (L) assesses executive functions of the brain such as organizational abilities, mental flexibility, and the ability to abstract and reason. These capacities are believed to be located in the frontal lobes. Damage to the frontal lobes can lead to abnormalities on this test.  The Blessed Rating Scale (C) is a tool that asks friends or family of the patient to assess the ability of the patient to function in his or her usual environment.  The WAIS-R (K) is an assessment of IQ used in ages 16 onward; it can be employed to help better understand the individual’s intellectual level of functioning and rule out an intellectual disability. IQ assessment will also aid the school in developing an individualized study program for the student.  The Rorschach Test (H) is a projective test that may be used to assess personality structure. The patient has characteristics of schizoid personality disorder, which may be better elucidated with a skilled assessment in the context of his clinical history.  The Folstein MMSE (E) is a quick, easily administered test that allows for immediate assessment of a major neurocognitive disorder (dementia). Scores of less than 24 are suggestive of dementia.  The MMPI-2 (F) is an objective test consisting of several hundred true/false questions used to assess an individual’s personality. It is the most widely used and highly standardized test of personality.  The Wada Test (J) is used to evaluate hemispheric language dominance prior to surgical amelioration of seizure focus. Whereas most right-handed individuals show left hemispheric dominance for language, left-handed individuals may be either right or left dominant. The test consists of injecting sodium amytal into the carotid artery and observing the transient effects on speech. Injection into the left carotid artery anesthetizes the left side of the brain, and those with left hemispheric language dominance show interrupted speech.  The Bender Gestalt Test (B) involves copying figures, which helps to screen for developmental disorders or brain damage.  The Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination (D) is a series of tests given by an experienced clinician to evaluate and make treatment recommendations for individuals with aphasia.  The Rey–Osterrieth figure (G) is sensitive to deficits in copying and lack of attention to detail in individuals with right-sided parietal lobe lesions.  The Stroop Test (I) assesses executive function as the patient has to deal with distractions and has to suppress an incorrect reply before providing the correct one.

options.text: Disclose the results in meeting with the patient and her parents.
Encourage the patient to discuss the results with her parents.
Notify the parents of the results because they pay her medical bills.
Report the results to Child Protective Services.

correct_answer.text: Encourage the patient to discuss the results with her parents.

correct_answers.text: Encourage the patient to discuss the results with her parents.

questions.explanation: Physician–patient confidentiality is an integral part of the physician–patient relationship and is especially important in establishing trust in therapeutic relationships. Confidentiality may be breached only in specific instances, such as the patient's waiving of the privilege (e.g., patient initiates litigation, consent to release information is obtained, there is a duty to protect, emergency situation, or in cases in which the court orders release). In this case, the information should not be released unless the patient has waived confidentiality privilege. Encouraging the minor to discuss the issue with her parents is the most appropriate step to respect confidentiality and promote trust.

questions.question_text: Which of the following woul be the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing major depressive disorder (MDD), single episode. Antidepressants are the treatment of choice. As this patient is showing some improvement and tolerating the medication, the most appropriate next step would first be to maximize the dose. Discontinuing his fluoxetine would greatly increase his risk of relapse.

questions.question_text: He eventually achieves full remission of his depressive symptoms and continues on the medication. However, he is concerned about his prognosis and potentially stopping the antidepressant in the future. What do you tell him is his approximate risk of developing further episode in the future?
questions.explanation: MDD tends to be a chronic illness. Patients with one episode of depression have a 50% risk of having future episodes, although antidepressants help to minimize the risk.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment of choice for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from major depressive disorder (MDD), with atypical features (i.e., increased appetite/sleep, mood reactivity). Because of their side effect profile, the treatment of choice in major depression is the serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as fluoxetine (Prozac). Amitriptyline and other tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) include the risk of arrhythmias and can be lethal in overdose, unlike the SSRIs. While the patient reports periods during which she is “just fine,” there is nothing to indicate a cycling pattern (i.e., bipolar disorder) that would require a mood stabilizer such as divalproex sodium. Similarly, being convinced that her fiancé is about to leave her is not likely psychotic, but is instead a distortion that does not require an antipsychotic such as ziprasidone. Although MAOIs such as phenelzine are thought to be somewhat more effective (than TCAs) in atypical depression, they carry the risk of hypertensive crisis when combined with foods containing tyramine.

She tells you she has just been married and would like to become pregnant. She and her husband have been having unprotected sex for 1 month. Ask how important pregnancy is to her.

Tell her to stop her medication entirely.

correct_answers.text: Discuss the risks and benefits of continuing her treatment during pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Fluoxetine is class C drug, meaning that it is potentially harmful to the developing fetus according to animal studies, although SSRIs are not believed to be teratogenic or cause birth defects. Therefore, a discussion of the risks and benefits of treatment is the most appropriate step.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the psychiatric emergency room by police after being found screaming while cutting down tree in the local park. He tells you that the ghost of his wife, who died 3 months ago, is living in the tree. The man has no previous psychiatric history, but he reports being very depressed since the death of his wife and has had suicidal ideation. He is disheveled and seems to have ignored his personal hygiene for some time. His vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most likely next course of action?
questions.explanation: This patient is exhibiting psychosis and depression. There are many possible etiologies, including major depressive disorder with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, schizoaffective disorder, and schizophrenia. Regardless of the eventual diagnosis, it is important to first rule out other causes such as illicit or prescribed drug intoxication. Therefore, it is premature to prescribe any medications for him.

correct_answers.text: Tell the mother to stop the St. John wort immediately.

questions.question_text: Which of the following side effects would be most important to discuss with the patient prior to starting?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine has a 7% risk of rash; unfortunately Stevens-Johnson syndrome (life-threatening rash) occurs in 0.1% of patients.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most significant factor mitigating her risk for suicide?
questions.explanation: Her lack of prior suicide attempts is her most significant protective factor.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medical conditions would be the most important to rule out as potential cause of depression in this patient?
questions.explanation: Many potential medical causes of depression, including thyroid dysfunction, vitamin B12 deficiency, renal disease, and vascular disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following do you most expect to find on her physical examination?
questions.explanation: This patient is most likely suffering from anorexia nervosa. Excessive mental activity is common in patients with anorexia or bulimia who are urged by self-induced vomiting. Cafe au lait spots are common in severe starvation.

questions.question_text: What is the likelihood that with treatment she will make full recovery over the next 10 years?
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa has variable course, although poor prognosis overall. Studies find only about 50% of patients have good outcome; 25% have poor outcome. Unfortunately, the mortality rate of anorexia nervosa is approximately 4%.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old graduate student presents to her University Health Care System with the chief complaint of “depression.” Upon detailed questioning she reveals a history of intense mood swings since early adolescence, with short (hours to days) periods of dysphoria, alternating with times where she feels “normal.” She admits that she is easily angered, occasionally breaking items and superficially cutting on herself when upset or bored. She has been unable to keep a boyfriend for more than several months, but states that she will frequently participate in “one-night stands” because she often feels lonely and empty. She denies persistent insomnia, anergia, or anhedonia, although she gets easily distracted while in lectures. While when acutely upset she may feel passively suicidal, she denies any past or current plan. Which of the following treatments would be the most appropriate to begin for this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient likely has borderline personality disorder. The first-line treatment for borderline personality disorder remains psychotherapy, such as DBT. DBT is a well-studied variation of CBT that focuses on suicidal behavior, consisting of individual psychotherapy, group therapy, and homework assignments. A variety of medications have been studied in borderline personality disorder, including antipsychotics (e.g., aripiprazole), antidepressants (e.g., citalopram), and mood stabilizers (e.g., lithium and valproic acid). However, while the listed medications have demonstrated some benefit in some of the symptoms of borderline personality disorder, in the absence of another psychiatric disorder (e.g., MDD, bipolar disorder), psychotherapy is the mainstay of treatment.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia presents to the emergency department. He had previously taken haloperidol (Haldol), but now refuses to take it. Because of this, you decide to try fluphenazine (Prolixin), which seems to mitigate his symptoms. One week later, he leaves the hospital. He continues the medications you prescribe and on a follow-up visit you notice he moves slowly and has a festinating gait. Blockade of which of the following receptors most likely accounts for the above side effect?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol and fluphenazine are first-generation antipsychotics (FGAs). The side effects described – moving slowly and a festinating gait – are extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), specifically parkinsonism. FGAs exert their antipsychotic effect primarily by blocking D2 dopamine receptors in the mesolimbic pathway (D), but they also block D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway (E). Blockade of D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway disrupts the balance of dopamine and acetylcholine in the basal ganglia, leading to EPS such as parkinsonism, dystonia, and akathisia. While acetylcholine receptors in the basal ganglia (A) are involved in the pathophysiology of EPS, the primary mechanism of action of FGAs causing these symptoms is dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. D4 receptors (B) are less relevant to the typical EPS seen with FGAs. 5-HT2 receptors (C) are primarily associated with the mechanism of action of atypical antipsychotics and are more related to reducing negative symptoms and atypical side effects.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old boy began having repetitive eye blinking at the age of 6. By age 12, he began blurting stereotypical phrases such as “Balls!” and “Shitty!” as well as making kissing noises. Concomitant with this, he has increasing difficulty with paying attention in school and occasionally displays wild, disinhibited behavior. Which of the following would be the most effective treatment for the primary (initial) condition?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of motor tics (eye blinking) starting at age 6, followed by vocal tics (stereotypical phrases and noises) by age 12, is characteristic of Tourette's Disorder. The associated 'wild, disinhibited behavior' and difficulty paying attention suggest co-occurring ADHD and potentially behavioral issues often seen with Tourette's. For Tourette's Disorder, the most effective treatments for tics are antipsychotics, specifically second-generation antipsychotics like risperidone (D), which are dopamine receptor blockers. Clonidine (A) is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that can be used for tics, especially in milder cases or when there is co-occurring ADHD, but antipsychotics are generally more effective for severe tics. Fluoxetine (B) is an antidepressant (SSRI) and would not be the primary treatment for tics. Methylphenidate (C) is a stimulant used for ADHD, and while ADHD is co-morbid, it's not the primary treatment for the tics themselves, and stimulants can sometimes exacerbate tics. Topiramate (E) is an anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer, not a primary treatment for Tourette's.

questions.question_text: A 12-year-old boy has recently been arrested for setting fire to a neighbor’s barn. He has been in trouble before for playing with fireworks in the neighborhood, and when he was 10 years old he was suspended for lighting matches at his school. Which of the following diagnoses would most likely be comorbid in this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of repetitive and escalating behaviors that violate the rights of others or major societal norms (setting fire to a barn, playing with fireworks, lighting matches at school) is highly indicative of Conduct Disorder. Conduct disorder is characterized by a persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms or rules are violated. Given his age (12), this diagnosis is appropriate. While other conditions might be comorbid, Conduct Disorder is the most direct and likely diagnosis based on the described actions. Pyromania, a specific impulse control disorder, could be considered, but Conduct Disorder encompasses a broader pattern of rule-breaking and aggressive behavior. Autism spectrum disorder (A), intellectual disability (C), major depressive disorder (D), and tic disorder (E) are less directly suggested by the primary behavioral issues presented.

questions.question_text: Which of the following interventions would be the most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The child is presenting with secondary enuresis (bedwetting after a period of dryness). Given the age and the normal developmental history, and the impact on his social life, the most appropriate initial intervention is behavioral therapy. This commonly includes techniques like enuresis alarms (bell and pad method) and motivational strategies (e.g., star charts). These methods help condition the child to wake up to a full bladder. Cognitive therapy and psychodynamic psychotherapy are generally not first-line treatments for enuresis. Punishment (E) is counterproductive and harmful.

questions.question_text: The child undergoes a lengthy trial of the recommended therapy as above, but his condition continues without significant improvement. Which of the following would be the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: While imipramine was considered the treatment of choice, because of its side effects (e.g., cardiotoxicity) desmopressin is considered first-line pharmacotherapy for enuresis. Although relapse is high after stopping the medication, approximately 30% of patients achieve total dryness, with another 40% exhibiting a reduction in bedwetting. Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant sometimes used as a mood stabilizer, and clonidine is an antihypertensive often used to treat opiate withdrawal and ADHD; neither are appropriate for the treatment of enuresis. Diphenhydramine is an antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, often used for insomnia or to treat extrapyramidal symptoms, and rarely used for enuresis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be this child’s most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Based on his academic difficulties and IQ, this patient would be classified as having mild intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder). Intellectual disability is characterized by deficits in intellectual functions confirmed by clinical assessment and standardized intelligence testing (e.g., IQ testing), as well as deficits in adaptive functioning that result in failure to meet developmental standards. While intellectual disabilities are common in patients with autistic spectrum disorder, there is no history of restrictive, repetitive patterns of behavior or interests consistent with autism.

questions.question_text: Given the above patient’s history, which of the following physical findings would most likely be expected?
questions.explanation: The key piece of history here is the 'biological mother with severe alcohol use disorder.' This strongly points to Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), of which Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS) is the most severe form. Characteristic physical findings of FAS include: facial dysmorphology (e.g., short palpebral fissures, thin vermilion border of the upper lip, smooth philtrum), growth deficits, and central nervous system abnormalities (including intellectual disability). Microcephaly (D), or a smaller-than-average head circumference, is a common neurological finding in FAS due to impaired brain development. While other conditions can cause intellectual disability and other physical findings, microcephaly is a hallmark physical manifestation of prenatal alcohol exposure in the context of intellectual disability. Cleft palate (A), congenital blindness (B), hyperextensible joints (C), and prominent jaw (E) are not typical characteristic physical findings of FAS.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old girl has come under the care of state Child Protection Services. Her mother was known to be using crack cocaine and IV heroin, and supporting her. The girl’s temporary foster parents reported to state workers that she was indiscriminately social with adults but often doesn’t appear to seek or respond to comforting. In her social interactions with other 5-year-old children at her preschool, she is noted to often stay by herself but is described as being inappropriately angry with her peers. Which of the following would be the most appropriate diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of coming under Child Protection Services due to maternal substance abuse, coupled with her observed behaviors (indiscriminate sociability with adults, not seeking or responding to comfort, social isolation from peers, and inappropriate anger), strongly points towards Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD). RAD is characterized by a pattern of inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behavior toward adult caregivers, and persistent social and emotional disturbance, including limited positive affect, minimal social and emotional responsiveness to others, and unexplained irritability, sadness, or fearfulness even during nonthreatening interactions with adult caregivers. While her mother's substance abuse is mentioned, the key diagnostic indicators are the child's relational and emotional difficulties. The other options are less fitting: ADHD (A) typically involves inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity; Autism spectrum disorder (B) involves deficits in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors, and while there's social difficulty, the indiscriminate friendliness with adults is inconsistent with classic autism; Conduct disorder(C) involves repetitive and persistent violations of the rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms, which is not the primary issue here; Language disorder (D) is a communication impairment, not directly indicated by these social behaviors.

questions.question_text: A 39-year-old man is arrested after being found in department store, disturbing by rubbing woman's shoes along his penis. He reluctantly admits that he has committed this act on numerous occasions although he has not gotten caught or arrested. He feels great deal of shame and guilt, but he is unable to stop the behavior. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Frotteuristic disorder is paraphilia characterized by the use of nonconsenting individuals for sexual gratification by rubbing against them.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most likely diagnosis for this ptient?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic

correct_answer.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic

correct_answers.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic

questions.explanation: Despite his recent diagnosis of a major depressive disorder (MDD), this patient has symptoms consistent with a current manic episode (e.g., euphoria, decreased need for sleep, impulsivity, pressured speech, impairment in functioning), and therefore would be diagnosed with bipolar disorder, current episode manic. Bipolar disorder, current episode depressed would be diagnosed in a patient with a history of mania but a current major depressive episode. Criteria for cyclothymic disorder are depressive episodes (which do not meet criteria for MDD) alternating with hypomanic episodes (symptoms of mania without impairment in functioning, psychotic symptoms, or the need for hospitalization). Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is a chronic, depressive illness, lasting for at least 2 years. Although the patient has manic symptoms and questionable psychosis (a grandiose delusion), there is no indication that he has had pervasive psychotic symptoms in the absence of his mood symptoms, which would be consistent with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: As this patient has symptoms consistent with bipolar I disorder, mania, he would most benefit from lithium or mood stabilizer such as valproic acid, or a typical antipsychotic (eg, olanzapine). Antidepressants such as citalopram, fluoxetine, and imipramine can exacerbate mania and should be avoided.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnoses would be the most appropriate in this ptient?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed
Major depressive disorder, with atypical features
Major depressive disorder, with melancholic features

correct_answer.text: Major depressive disorder, with atypical features

correct_answers.text: Major depressive disorder, with atypical features

questions.explanation: A major depressive episode with atypical features is characterized by mood reactivity, rejection sensitivity, hypersomnia, increased appetite, and 'leaden paralysis' (ie, heavy feeling in extremities).

questions.question_text: Which of the following classes of medications would be the most effective in this patient?
questions.explanation: Although not commonly used because of the risk of side effects, MAOIs are considered to be the most effective drugs for treating atypical depression, especially compared to TCAs.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnoses is the most appropriate for this ptient?
questions.explanation: This case deliberately brings together many character traits drawn from “pure” diagnoses of personality (character) disorders, including borderline, narcissistic, dependent, obsessive-compulsive, and schizotypal personalities. In clinical practice, many patients do not meet criteria for any one specific personality disorder; such mixed cases are referred to as other specified personality disorder. Patients with diagnosed borderline personality disorder are known for their intense personal relationships, mood lability, self-destructive behaviors, anger management issues, and a poor sense of self-image. Narcissistic personality disorder is marked by a grandiose sense of self-worth, entitlement, lack of real empathy, and a tendency to use others for one’s own ends. Patients with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder are perfectionists, inflexible, and overly demanding of themselves and others. Schizotypal patients are known for their quirkiness and seemingly magical thinking styles.

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old woman is hospitalized during psychotic episode in which she has the delusion that she is being controlled with computer programs developed by the Department of Homeland Security. According to her family, she stopped taking her regimen of quetiapine and lithium 4 weeks before this admission to the hospital, and she has been telling her family about her concerns regarding the government controlling her for the last 2 weeks. The patient's past psychiatric history is significant for three prior hospitalizations over the last 20 years. At the time of her first admission, she presented with 3-week history of chronic symptoms and psychosis. During her second hospitalization, she was noted to be depressed with psychotic symptoms. During her third admission, she was again depressed with prominent disorganized behavior. Her mental status examination upon presentation to the hospital reveals loosening of association and delusion-like symptoms without prominent mood component.

options.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) with psychotic features

questions.explanation: The essential features of schizophrenia include prominent positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations), disorganized behavior without prominent mood component, and continuous signs of illness for at least 6 months.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is most likely to cause this ptient’s confusion?
questions.explanation: Delirium related to blockade of cholinergic receptors is the most common cause of medication-induced delirium in the elderly. Cimetidine, an H2 receptor antagonist, has anticholinergic properties.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurotransmitter systems is most directly implicated in the etiology of her confusion?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter most implicated in cognitive functioning. Anticholinergic effects of medications are frequently implicated in cognitive decline and drug-induced delirium.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has good benefit with antipsychotic medications but is poorly compliant due to lack of insight and reduced cognition.
questions.explanation: Patients with mental illnesses may be noncompliant for various reasons. Long-acting antipsychotics such as risperidone Consta (K) are good choices in psychotic patients who benefit from and tolerate antipsychotics, but who are noncompliant due to lack of insight, confusion, or forgetfulness (not due to side effects).  Chlorpromazine (C) is a typical antipsychotic (neuroleptic) which has been associated with sensitivity to sunlight, which can cause an exaggerated sunburn.  Clozapine (D) was the first “atypical” antipsychotic developed; it is approved for the treatment of patients with refractory schizophrenia and has also demonstrated efficacy in reducing suicidality in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.    Bupropion (B) is an antidepressant that is believed to block reuptake of dopamine in the brain. Although all antidepressant medications have similar efficacy, including nortriptyline (H) (tricyclic antidepressant), paroxetine (I) and sertraline (L) (serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors), and venlafaxine (N) (combined serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), only bupropion has a reduced risk of sexual dysfunction, and in fact may be used to treat antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction.    While no psychotropic medications are proven safe in pregnancy, antimanic agents such as carbamazepine, lithium (G), and valproic acid (M) are associated with significant fetal abnormalities and should be avoided. Haloperidol (E) has been used safely in pregnant patients with bipolar disorder.    Lamotrigine (F) is an antiepileptic medication indicated for the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder (to delay the time to occurrence of mood episodes) and for the acute treatment of bipolar depression.    Aripiprazole (A) and risperidone (J) are second-generation antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: A clinical research psychiatrist at university A has been running double-blind placebo-controlled trial of new antidepressant. The psychiatrist concludes after statistical analysis of the data that there is no better effect of the drug compared to placebo. The psychiatrist's colleagues at five separate institutions (universities B, C, D, E, and F) have run identical studies and determine that there is treatment effect of the drug compared to placebo. Given this information, one may conclude that the research trial at university A resulted in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Studies that find no statistically significant difference between groups when there is a difference result in type II error. In this case, the positive findings at the other universities make the finding at university A less likely to be correct.

questions.question_text: Which of the following side effects is most consistent with this case?
questions.explanation: This case most consistent with tardive dyskinesia, an extrapyramidal syndrome that usually effects distal limb or facial musculature and causes choreiform or athetoid movements. Its onset is usually several years after initiating antipsychotics and more likely to affect older patients.

questions.question_text: Which of the following anatomic structures is most likely implicated in the etiology of his movements?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia, responsible for the transmission of thought to action and for controlling the initiation and quality of motor action, is central to the pathophysiology of extrapyramidal syndromes, including dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most beneficial for this patient?
questions.explanation: Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker, has demonstrated significant efficacy in treating many of the symptoms of PTSD (e.g., nightmares, flashbacks, hyperarousal, violence).

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old married man presents to your outpatient psychiatric clinic complaining of anxiety and depression. His social history reveals that he is junior faculty member of a local university, working about 60 hours per week. He enjoys his job but reports stress rising from his marital relationship because his wife accuses him of not spending 'quality time' with her and his being 'married to the job.' According to Erik Erikson, in which stage of development does this patient currently have conflict?
questions.explanation: Erik Erikson described eight stages of human psychological experience running the entire lifespan. This patient is in the stage of intimacy versus isolation (age 21–40 years) and is having difficulty with intimacy in his relationship.

questions.question_text: Which of the following additional symptoms would be most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation: Hyperreligious thinking or preoccupation with moral behavior, altered sexual behaviors, hypergraphia or overspending of the selves and others, and heightened experience of emotions are classic signs associated with complex partial seizures (temporal lobe seizures).

questions.question_text: A sleep-deprived electroencephalogram is performed on the patient as part of his complete workup. Which of the following lobes of the brain would most likely demonstrate abnormalities in this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient most likely would demonstrate seizure activity in his temporal lobes, consistent with temporal lobe epilepsy.

questions.question_text: After being called to the emergency department to evaluate young woman who overdosed on barbiturates, you find her in bed with her eyes close. She opens her eyes briefly in response to pain and demonstrates flexion from pain but makes no sounds. Which of the following best represents her Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale measures level of arousal and ranges from scale of 3 (deep coma) to 14 (fully alert). The categories assessed are eye opening, best motor response, and best verbal response. Eye opening range from score of 4 (opening spontaneously) to 1 (not opening at all). In this case, the eyes open to pain, so score of 2 is given. Best motor response is as follows: obeys commands, 5; localizes pain, 4; flexion, 3; extension, 2; and no response, 1. In this case, score of 3 is given for the response. Best verbal response is also based on scale ranging from 5 to 1. An oriented patient receives a score of 5 and no response receives a score of 1, as in this case. The scores are then added, and in this case are 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the best strategy in making the transition from the SSRI to the MAOI?

options.text: Begin tapering the dose of the SSRI while increasing the dose of the MAOI simultaneously.
Start the MAOI until the therapeutic levels have been reached, then taper the SSRI.
Stop the SSRI brutally and begin the MAOI at nonequivalent dose the following day.
Stop the SSRI brutally and initiate MAOI.
Taper the SSRI and 5 weeks after the last dose begin the MAOI.

correct_answer.text: Taper the SSRI and 5 weeks after the last dose begin the MAOI.

correct_answers.text: Taper the SSRI and 5 weeks after the last dose begin the MAOI.

questions.explanation: When changing from an SSRI to an MAOI, one must allow washout period of about five half-lives for the SSRI to be more than 90% eliminated; in the case of fluoxetine, this is approximately 5 weeks. This precaution avoids the serotonin syndrome, which may occur when significant blood levels of both drugs are present. Serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal, is marked by symptoms of tremor, diaphoresis, rigidity, myoclonus, autonomic dysregulation, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and coma. The other choices would pose significant risk of developing serotonin syndrome.

questions.question_text: After he is switched to the phenelzine, which of the following foods/drink should the patient most avoid?
questions.explanation: MAOIs prevent the peripheral breakdown of tyramine, which may be ingested with certain foods such as liver, beer, red wine, aged cheeses, smoked fish, dry sausage, and fava beans. If too much tyramine builds up in the blood, it may saturate peripheral sympathetic nerve receptors and cause hypertensive crisis, potentially fatal condition. The other choices do not contribute to hypertensive crisis.

questions.question_text: A 66-year-old man with history of schizophrenia has been on thioridazine (Mellaril) 700 mg qd for many years, after numerous unsuccessful trials with various antipsychotics. Over the last 8 months, he has been complaining of hearing derogatory voices, and his dose has been gradually increased to 1,000 mg qd. He has no signs of tardive dyskinesia. Which of the following side effects would be the most concerning at this dose?
questions.explanation: Thioridazine is typical neuroleptic, rarely used now due to the risk of cardiac arrhythmias. At doses of 1,000 mg/d or higher, thioridazine has been associated with pigmentary retinopathy, also known as retinitis pigmentosa. Therefore, doses should not exceed 800 mg/d. Pigmentary retinopathy can cause loss of retinal response to contraction of the visual field. An early sign may be nocturnal confusion. Constipation, dry eyes, and urinary retention are all side effects from the anticholinergic properties of thioridazine, but typically are not so severe as to compromise health permanently. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is not associated with thioridazine.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man without prior psychiatric history is admitted to the psychiatric ward with disorganization, paranoia, agitation, and continuous auditory hallucinations telling him to kill himself. He is given two doses of haloperidol 5 mg orally. Approximately 8 hours later, he develops torticollis. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction from the haloperidol, high-potency first-generation (typical) antipsychotic, typically seen hours to days after initiating or increasing the antipsychotic. Acute dystonic reactions may present as muscle spasms, torticollis, oculogyric crisis, and laryngeal spasms. Benztropine 1 to 2 mg IM is useful in the treatment of acute dystonic reactions. Alternatively, diphenhydramine 50 mg IM can also be used. If the symptoms do not resolve within 20 minutes, larger doses can be given. Benzodiazepines can also be used but are not first-line treatment. For acute laryngeal dystonia, larger doses of benztropine should be given immediately, followed by lorazepam IV if needed. None of the other choices are indicated for the treatment of acute dystonia. While nonsteroidal analgesics such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen may help with pain, they won't resolve the underlying etiology. Cyclobenzaprine is a muscle relaxer which will not adequately treat the dystonia. Propranolol is a β-blocker, used for hypertension, but it can also be used to treat akathisia, another side effect of antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman with history of bipolar disorder is admitted to the medical service because of weakness, mental status changes, and serum sodium of 154 mmol/L. According to her boyfriend, for the last 2 weeks she has been drinking "lots and lots of water" but complaining of being thirsty often, and also of frequently urinating. Which of the following medications would be most likely responsible for this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: The disorder described is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, most likely caused by lithium. Lithium inhibits the effect of antidiuretic hormone on the kidney, causing polyuria, thirst, polydipsia, and potential hypernatremia. Although carbamazepine and valproic acid (other mood stabilizers), haloperidol (first-generation antipsychotic), and quetiapine (second-generation antipsychotic) are all used to treat bipolar disorder, none are associated with diabetes insipidus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most appropraite to treat his withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Clonidine, central alpha-2-autoreceptor agonist, has been proven useful in the treatment of the autonomic hyperactivity associated with opioid withdrawal. Antabuse is used to treat Parkinson disease and also as an anti-influenza agent. Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, and lorazepam, benzodiazepine, may help with significant agitation occasionally seen in withdrawal, but they will not treat the underlying symptoms. Naloxone, opioid antagonist, is used in opioid overdose and will significantly worsen opioid withdrawal symptoms in this patient.

questions.question_text: After the patient completes his detoxification on the unit, he continues to be motivated to abstain from heroin use. He is referred to an outpatient addictions program, but wishes to take medication to decrease his heroin use after discharge. Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate to prescribe?
questions.explanation: Methadone has been proven to significantly reduce the use of heroin when used maintenance medication. Patients maintenance on doses lower than 40 mg/d of methadone are more likely to relapse than those on higher doses. Dantrolene is muscle-relaxant used in the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, rare side effect of antipsychotic treatment. Disulfiram is medication used to prevent alcohol consumption by causing an aversive reaction if taken in conjunction with alcohol. Flumazenil is benzodiazepine antagonist used in the emergency treatment of overdose with benzodiazepines, which does not cause withdrawal. Sertraline, an SSRI, is antidepressant and will not help with agitation. While it may be helpful for comorbid depression or anxiety, it has not been shown to decrease opioid use in individuals.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants should be most avoided in this particular patient?
questions.explanation: Imipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA). TCAs are considered class 1A antiarrhythmics because they possess quinine-like effects that decrease conduction time through the bundle of His. They have been shown to increase mortality in cardiac patients. TCAs can also increase the heart rate, and so patients with compromised cardiac function may suffer from increased oxygen demand. Finally, TCAs are also associated with significant orthostatic hypotension, which may be further exacerbate in patients with cardiac disease. Wellbutrin, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (such as mirtazapine and venlafaxine), and serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like sertraline all be safely used in patients with cardiac disease; however, attention should be paid to potential hypertension cause or worsened by venlafaxine and any cardiac medicines metabolize through the P-450 cytochrome system, as some SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine) may alter the medication levels.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants would most likely result in cognitive decline in this patient?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter most implicated in cognitive functioning. Anticholinergic effects of medications are frequently implicated in cognitive decline and drug-induced delirium. Of the medications listed, paroxetine has the most anticholinergic effect, and therefore should be avoided in this patient with major neurocognitive disorder (dementia).

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder and frequent hospitalizations presents to the emergency department after taking an overdose of lithium in a suicide attempt. Which of the following signs would be most likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Lithium toxicity is characterized early on by dysarthria, ataxia, coarse tremor, and abnormal lithium. Later manifestations include seizures, neuromuscular irritability, and impaired consciousness (delirium to coma). Acute dystonias are associated with the use of typical antipsychotics. Leg pain and paresthesias are not associated with lithium. Paranoid delusions are rare of the symptom profile of schizophrenia in some cases of bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following minimum duration should the seizure last for optimal effectiveness in this patient?
questions.explanation: For ECT to be effective, the seizure should last at least 15 seconds. Prolonged seizures greater than 180 seconds should be terminated with an anesthetic (e.g., propofol) or intravenous benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam).

questions.question_text: Which of the following adverse effects would be the most likely during the course of ECT?
questions.explanation: Memory impairment (mostly during the treatment) is quite common, although most patients return to their baseline by 6 months. There is no indication that ECT causes brain damage. ECT may actually be used to treat patients with catatonia. Fractures and vomiting are uncommonly seen in ECT since the use of muscle relaxants and anesthetics have been implemented.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the best immediate treatment for the agitation in this patient?
questions.explanation: For extreme agitation, the benzodiazepine lorazepam can be effective. Another alternative is the butyrophenone antipsychotic haloperidol. Phenothiazine antipsychotics such as chlorpromazine can cause untoward instability when given to patients with PCP intoxication. Trazodone, an antidepressant, and fluoxetine, an SSRI, are antidepressants, and will not help with agitation. Trihexyphenidyl is used to combat extrapyramidal symptoms associated with antipsychotic use and not for agitated states.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments would be the most appropriate if this patient were not agitated?
questions.explanation: Supportive care is the best treatment for PCP intoxication that is not complicated by extreme agitation or violence. Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, or haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic, can be useful for extreme agitation. Acidification of the urine does not significantly increase the excretion of PCP. Despite urban myths, neither cheese nor vitamins have particular therapeutic benefits for PCP intoxication.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with prior history of major depression is admitted to the psychiatric inpatient ward. She has been severely depressed, with poor sleep, decreased appetite, low energy, and suicidal ideation. She now believes that her neighbors are conspiring to murder her, and occasionally can hear her neighbors' voice that tells her she should die. After seeking with the neighbors, you find out that they brought her to the hospital. They have been good friends for 20 years and have noticed the patient has not been leaving the house much, has taken to looking out of her windows with suspicious glances, and has not cleaned her house in the last 2 months. Which of the following medication combinations would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient is most likely suffering from major depressive disorder with psychotic features. Neither antidepressants nor antipsychotics alone will substantially or effectively treat major depression with psychotic features, so the combination is preferred. The combination of lorazepam and clozapine (an atypical antipsychotic) will not properly treat the depression. Similarly, the combination of sertraline and lorazepam will not adequately treat the psychotic symptoms nor depression. Lithium and synthroid can both effectively augment antidepressants such as paroxetine and sertraline. Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, may help with anxiety, but will not be effective against psychosis or depression.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by the police. He shows agitation, vertical nystagmus, and analgesia.
questions.explanation: PCP (nicknamed "angel dust") intoxication produces agitation, vertical nystagmus, and analgesia as well as hyperthermia, euphoria, visual hallucinations, catatonia, and visual olfactory abnormalities.

questions.question_text: A 62-year-old homeless man admitted to psychiatric unit begins having elevated vital signs, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, tremor, and seizures.
questions.explanation: Alcohol withdrawal may begin within 24 hours after the last drink and can progress to seizures by 24 to 48 hours and delirium tremens (DTs) after approximately 72 hours. DTs are associated with significant risk of mortality.

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old woman presents to the psychiatric emergency department complaining of depression and suicidality. She is observed to be fatigued, irritable, and with dysphoric affect.
questions.explanation: The symptoms associated with cocaine withdrawal tend to be ill and last several days after the last use. Occasionally, however, the depression can be severe enough to raise the risk of self-injurious behavior or suicide attempts.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old musician presents in the outpatient clinic. He complains of fever and chills, runny nose, nausea, body aches, diarrhea, and myalgias for the last 24 hours.
questions.explanation: Heroin withdrawal peaks at about 72 hours after the last use in chronic users. It is experienced as severe flu-like symptoms and gastrointestinal complaints, such as fever and chills, runny nose, nausea, body aches, diarrhea, and myalgias. The occurrence of piloerection in the syndrome gave rise to the slang term "cold turkey" to describe the action of total cessation of use of the drug.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia presents with fever and chills. He is found to be bacteremic and has a WBC count of 900/µL.
questions.explanation: Clozapine (an atypical neuroleptic) causes agranulocytosis in about 1% of patients. For this reason, weekly blood counts are measured for the first 6 months of treatment, every 2 weeks for the next 6 months, then every 4 weeks thereafter (unless there is significant reduction in white blood cell counts).

questions.question_text: A 41-year-old woman on medications for her bipolar disorder presents with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and decreased concentration.
questions.explanation: Lithium is associated with clinical hypothyroidism in at least 5% of patients, significantly more often in women. Thyroid supplementation may be needed to counter this side effect. Approximately 25% to 30% of patients may show elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone levels.
